hookLine: On the morning of the twenty-seventh of January, two thousand and one, a young woman in Connellsville, Pennsylvania told police officers where she had been the night before.

captions.text:
On the morning of the twenty-seventh of January,
two thousand and one,
a young woman in Connellsville,

Pennsylvania told police officers where she
had been the night before.

She told them how she had got the marks
on her face and on her foot.

Her cousin said the same. Her sisters said
the same. So did the man she was seeing.

Within weeks the laboratory said the same, twice
over —

the blood on her shirt was his, and nothing
at the scene was hers.

Then a man came forward twenty months late
and took it back on the stand.
A dentist said she could not tell.
A second expert said he could,

and when the timing did not work he changed
the timing without looking
at anything new.
Fifteen years after that first morning,

another expert examined the photographs taken
of her injuries that day,
and reported that she had been telling the truth.

By then Crystal Weimer had been in prison for more
than eleven years.

Nobody ever found anything. This is what happened
in between. Not the trial.

The trial takes four minutes to describe and it
is the least surprising part of it.

What is worth the time is the seven years
before the arrest,

and the eleven years after it, and how little
either of them required.

Connellsville sits in Fayette County,
in the south-west corner of Pennsylvania,

where the hills start to fold. It is a small
place.
Small enough that a case does not stay quiet,
because the people in it already know each other.

In the early hours of the twenty-seventh
of January,

officers from the Connellsville Police Department
went to the apartment

of a man named Curtis Haith. They found him
outside on the pavement.

He had been beaten. He had been shot in the face.
Curtis Haith was twenty-one.
He wanted to be a chef.

At the officers' request, the District Attorney
came to the apartment herself.
Her name was Nancy Vernon,
and she had been the elected District Attorney
of Fayette County since the early nineties.

She took part in the investigation and helped
direct it,
that morning and for years afterwards.

That detail matters later, and not for the reason
it might seem to.
A prosecutor who advocates in court is protected

by something called absolute immunity — she cannot
be sued for it,
however wrong she turns out to be.

A prosecutor who acts as an investigator
is not protected in the same way.

Where the line between those two things falls,
in this case,

took a federal appeals court twenty years
to reach.
Inside, the search recovered DNA samples.

It also recovered a significant amount
of drug-related evidence.

That second finding gave the investigation
its early shape.

A man beaten and shot outside an apartment
with drugs in it, in a small town,

on a night when the apartment had been full
of people.

The neighbours told police that Haith
had been out that night,

and that a dozen or more people had passed
through his apartment between the evening

of the twenty-sixth and the morning
of the twenty-seventh.
So the officers began working through the list.

Everyone who had been at those parties. One
after another.

Where they had been, who they had left with, what
time they got home.

That is ordinary police work and there is nothing
wrong with it.

A dozen people is a dozen people. Some of them
will remember badly.

Some of them will have reasons of their own
to be careful about what they say.

The job is to keep going until the accounts either
fit together or they do not.

An investigation that begins with a dozen equal
names ends with one of them.

Something has to do the narrowing. Physical
evidence can do it. A witness can do it.
So can nothing at all,

if one name simply stays in the file longer
than the others and starts
to look like an answer.

On the twenty-seventh of January nothing
had narrowed anything.

Everyone on that list had been somewhere the night
before. Everyone had an account.

Not one of those accounts had yet been set
against anything outside itself.

Where the narrowing came from is the whole
of this story.

One of the people on that list was a woman called
Crystal Weimer.

She had three young daughters, and she was raising
the three of them on her own.
When they arrived at her house that morning,

she was still wearing the clothes she had worn
the night before.

She had a minor injury to her face. She
had a minor injury to her foot.

There was what looked like mud on her clothes,
and what looked like blood.

She told them her account without being asked
twice. She had been at the party.

She had given Haith a ride and dropped him
at another party.

After that she had gone to the housing community
where her mother

and her sisters lived, and stayed there.
Her cousin confirmed it.

Her sisters confirmed it. Michael Gibson, the man
she was seeing, confirmed it.
She explained the injuries too.

The foot was from horseplaying with Gibson a few
days earlier.

The eye, and the blood on the shirt,
were from a fight with Gibson.

That was the account she gave
on the twenty-seventh of January,

two thousand and one. Where she was. Who she
was with. How she got the marks.
It is worth being precise about what happened

to that account over the following fifteen years,
because the answer is nothing.
She did not revise it.

She did not offer a second version when the first
one stopped working,

because it never stopped working. Every other
account in this case moves.

Hers does not. Then the laboratory results came
back.

The blood on Crystal Weimer's clothes was Michael
Gibson's blood.

Exactly as she had said. None of the DNA collected
from the crime scene matched her.

Not one sample. And the samples that were there
suggested something else.
They suggested a male profile.

That is the whole of the physical evidence,
on the twenty-seventh of January,

two thousand and one. It points away from her. It
does not point at her once.
And it corroborated her, twice over.

She had said the blood was Gibson's, and it
was Gibson's.

She had said she had not been there when Haith
was killed,
and nothing at the scene carried her.

A laboratory result has a property that nothing
else in this case has.
It does not change with retelling,

and it was produced before anybody had a theory
to protect.

There are two findings inside it and they
do different work.
The first is an exclusion.
None of the crime-scene samples were hers,
and what was there suggested a male profile.

An exclusion is not proof that a person
was somewhere else.
It does mean the scene carried nothing of her.

The second is a confirmation, and it is the rarer
of the two.

She had named the source of the blood on her own
shirt on the first morning,

before any testing existed. The testing agreed
with her.

A false account does not usually hand
the laboratory the one thing

that can break it. And then nothing happened.
The file stayed open.

The investigation did not close and it
did not move. Winter went. Spring came.
The town did what towns do. Nobody was charged.

Nobody was cleared either,
and those are not the same thing.

Being uncharged is not a finding. It
is an absence.

The people who had been interviewed that January
stayed interviewed,

and stayed in a small town where everyone knew
who the police had spoken to.
Curtis Haith's family waited.

That is the part of an unsolved killing
that does not get filmed.

Somebody's son had been shot in the face
on a pavement, and the months went past,

and there was nothing to tell them. Twenty months
went by like that.

In October of two thousand and two, a man named
Thomas Beal went to the police.

Weimer had dated Beal before she was seeing
Gibson.

What he told officers was that Weimer and Gibson
had killed Curtis Haith.

According to Beal, Weimer had told him something
specific.

She had told him that the blood on her clothes
was Haith's.

The DNA had already established, twenty months
earlier,
that the blood on her clothes was Gibson's.

So the first statement against her contained
a fact
that the evidence had already ruled out.
There was a second half to what Beal reported,

and the two halves are not the same kind of claim.
The first half was the blood.

That is checkable, and it had been checked, twenty
months before he said it.

The second half was that Weimer and Gibson
had killed Curtis Haith.
Nothing can be set beside that.
No sample answers it, and no record answers it,

and no document answers it either way.
So the statement arrived in two pieces.
One of them failed on the day it was made.

The other could not be made to fail,
because nothing could reach it —

and that was the piece that stayed in the case
for the next three and a half years.

There is a straightforward test available
at that moment, and it costs nothing.

A witness reports a confession. The confession
contains a checkable detail.
Check it.

If the detail is wrong, the witness either
misremembered, or was told wrong,

or is making it up — and you find
out which before you build on him.
The detail was wrong. Beal was not set aside.
The investigation now had a direction,

and the direction was a woman whose physical
evidence had cleared her twenty months
earlier. Around the same time,

the Pennsylvania State Police Cold Case Squad
began to assist.

A cold case unit exists because old files go stale
in a particular way.

The people who worked them move on, memories
harden,
and the evidence stops being re-examined.

So a new team comes in with fresh eyes and looks
again at what is already
in the box. The strength of that is obvious.
The weakness is less obvious and it is this:

a fresh look at old material is still a look
at old material. Nothing arrives.

What changes is who is reading it, and what they
are reading it for. New people.
The same file. And now a name to test it against.

One of them went back through the autopsy
photographs of Curtis Haith's body.

And on his hand, she saw something she believed
was a bite mark.
Those photographs were not new.

They were taken at the autopsy, at the start
of the case,
and they had been in the file ever since.

The bite mark enters this case in the autumn
of two thousand and two.
Nothing about the photograph changed in between.
What changed was who was reading it,

and what else was sitting in the file beside it
by then.
That is not a criticism of looking again.
Looking again is what a cold case squad is for,

and sometimes the second reader is the one
who is right.

It only fixes the order of events. The accusation
came first.

A bite mark is not a fingerprint, and it
was not treated as one even then.

The comparison works by taking impressions
of a suspect's teeth
and matching the pattern to the injury.

So it depends on how the mark was left, and on how
the skin behaved afterwards.

And it depends on the judgement of the person
doing the looking.
It is the judgement that carries it.

A dentist in Fayette County was asked to analyse
the injury. She looked at it.

She compared it against teeth impressions. And she
reached a conclusion.

Her conclusion was that Michael Gibson had bitten
Curtis Haith.

Then she was given impressions of Crystal Weimer's
teeth as well,
and asked to look again.
After that comparison,

she reported that she could not identify which set
of teeth had caused the mark.

Read that sequence slowly, because the order of it
is the whole point.
The first look produced a name.

The second look, with more material, produced less
certainty rather than more.

The honest answer, and she gave it,
was that the mark did not tell her who made it.
That should have been the end of the bite mark.
An examiner looked at the physical evidence twice,
with more information the second time,
and reported that it did not identify anybody.
A piece of evidence

that cannot distinguish between two people
is not evidence against either of them.

That is where the dentist stopped. She said she
could not tell.
So a different expert was brought in.
Here is what that expert was given to work with.
Photographs of the injury to Haith's hand.

Teeth impressions from Gibson and from Weimer.
And Thomas Beal's statement.

He read the accusation, and then he examined
the evidence.
That order is not a small thing.

The point of a physical comparison is that it
can disagree with the story.
If the story arrives first,

the comparison has been given somewhere to land
before it has looked at anything.
Set the two examinations beside each other.

The dentist had the injury and two sets
of impressions.

She produced a name, then withdrew it, and ended
with no identification at all.

The second expert had photographs of the same
injury and the same two sets

of impressions. One item in his materials
was not in hers.

It was Thomas Beal's statement, and a statement
is not physical evidence.
It cannot be compared with anything.
What it can do is tell a reader

which of the two available answers is the one
being looked for. Same injury.

The same two sets of teeth. One extra document,
and a different result.

His conclusion was that the bite mark matched
Crystal Weimer.

One dentist had said Gibson. Then she had said she
could not tell.

The next expert said Weimer, and he had been given
the name first.

That is the physical case. There is nothing else
in it.

A problem surfaced with the bite mark, and it
was a serious one.
Nobody could say when it had happened.

A bite on a hand could have been left hours
before a man died.
It could have been left days before.

If it was days before, it proved nothing
about the night of the murder at all.

So the question of timing was put back
to the investigation.
Vernon directed officers to look into it,

and the expert was asked to update his opinion. He
did.

He determined that the bite had occurred seven
to ten minutes
before Curtis Haith's death.

He reached that conclusion without reviewing any
additional evidence.

Nothing new had been found. Nothing new
had been tested.

The same photographs, the same impressions,
the same man.

A question was asked, and the answer moved. Seven
to ten minutes.

Close enough to put her there at the moment he
died.
Consider what that number would require.

Not that the bite happened around the same time
as the killing.

That it happened inside a window of about three
minutes.
Identified from a photograph of a mark on skin.
By a man who had already given his opinion once,
and was being asked whether he could make it fit.

There is a version
of this that would have been unremarkable.
An expert goes back to his materials,

finds something in them he had not weighed
the first time,

reports that it narrows the timing, and says what
he looked at to get there.

That happens. It is ordinary work. The record
does not describe that.

It describes an opinion updated without additional
evidence.

An opinion that can move without new material
can move again.

Whatever produced that number, it
was not the material,

because the material was identical
before and after.

Meanwhile investigators went back to Thomas Beal.
He had a new version.

He now said that a third person had taken part
in the murder.
A man he called Lonnie.

Officers investigated the name, at the direction
of the police and of Vernon.
They established what had happened to Lonnie.

At the time Curtis Haith was killed, Lonnie
was incarcerated.

That is one of the few things in a criminal case
that settles without argument.
Custody records are dated.
They do not rest on anybody's memory,

or on anybody's reason for remembering it
a particular way.
Beal had added a third person to the murder.

The third person was locked up on the night it
happened.

The court that later reviewed all of this wrote
one sentence about what followed.
"Despite these puzzling changes to his story,

Beal remained a key witness." In August of two
thousand and three —
two and a half years after the murder now —

a prisoner named Conrad Blair contacted
the police.
Blair said that a fellow inmate, Joseph Stenger,
had confessed to being involved in Haith's death.

Vernon and a Connellsville officer went
to interview him.

Blair told them that Stenger, Weimer and Beal
had killed Curtis Haith.

He also handed over a written statement. He said
Stenger had written it.
The statement did not say what Blair said it said.

In the statement, Stenger was not involved
in the killing at all.
He had only helped dispose of evidence, in a pond.

On the strength of that, Vernon helped assemble
a dive team,
and they searched the pond.

Vernon and several officers also met
with Stenger's attorney.

The attorney told them his client had not written
the statement.

The record of this case does not say what
the divers found in the pond.
It does not need to.
By the time they were in the water,

the document that sent them there had already
been disowned
by the man whose name was on it,

and it had already contradicted the man
who produced it. Three accusations now.

Beal, who had described blood the DNA had already
ruled out,

and then added a man who was in prison. Blair,
whose document contradicted him.

Stenger, who had not written what was attributed
to him.
None of it agreed with any of the rest of it.
And it is worth saying what was not there.

No physical evidence tying Crystal Weimer
to the scene —

that had been settled in two thousand and one.
No confession from her. No weapon.

No witness who put her at the apartment when Haith
was killed.

What existed was three men who had come forward
at different times
with incompatible accounts,

and one comparison whose timing had been adjusted
after the fact.

There is a pattern in where those men
were standing when they spoke.

Beal came in of his own accord, twenty months
late,

with a detail that had already been disproved.
Blair was in prison.
Stenger was in prison.

Everything that pointed at Crystal Weimer came
from someone with a reason

to be talking to the police, and nothing
that pointed at her came from the scene.

None of that makes any of them liars. People
in custody tell the truth all the time.

It only means that each account needed checking
against something outside itself —
and each time one was checked, it failed.
In late December of two thousand and three,

officers prepared a criminal complaint charging
Crystal Weimer with the murder
of Curtis Haith.

The court that later reviewed the case described
the moment in one clause.

The complaint was prepared "despite
the conflicting statements from Beal, Blair,
and Stenger". Nancy Vernon approved it.

In January of two thousand and four, three years
after Haith died,
Crystal Weimer was arrested.

The court that reviewed all of this described what
happened next in seven words.

"The case against Weimer fell apart almost
immediately." A preliminary hearing
is not a trial.
It is a low bar, deliberately:

the Commonwealth has only to show that a crime
happened and that there is enough

to believe this defendant did it. Cases
are not supposed to end there.

She was defended by the Fayette County Public
Defender's Office.

A private defence would have cost around fifty
thousand dollars,
and she did not have fifty thousand dollars.

That is not unusual and it is not a scandal
on its own.

It only means that everything that follows
happened to somebody
who could not buy her way out of any part of it.
At that hearing,

the Commonwealth called Thomas Beal to the stand
as a witness of fact.
Under oath, Beal took it all back.
He testified that an officer had — his words —

"kind of like coaxed me along on how to do it."
The judge dismissed the charges.

Crystal Weimer went home. She was home for six
months.

"Nevertheless, investigators continued to focus
their efforts on Weimer." In July

of two thousand and four, Joseph Stenger made
an offer.

He told police he would implicate Weimer
in the murder.

In exchange, he wanted a lighter sentence
on convictions of his own,
in an unrelated matter.
On the strength of that statement,

officers arrested Crystal Weimer for a second time
and charged her again.
This time it went to trial.

The trial ran in Fayette County in the spring
of two thousand and six.

The Commonwealth's case was the case it had always
been.
The bite mark, with its timing. And the witnesses.

Among the witnesses were men who were in custody
at the time they came forward.
Jailhouse informants.

Juries are generally sceptical of them,
for the obvious reason,

and the standard way to handle that is to put
the question directly:

are you getting anything for this? They
were asked.

They told the jury they were not receiving deals
in exchange for their testimony.
On the seventh of April, two thousand and six,

the jury convicted Crystal Weimer of third-degree
murder and of conspiracy
to commit murder.
Third-degree murder, in Pennsylvania,

is a killing done with malice but without
a specific intent to kill.

Conspiracy means an agreement with somebody else
to commit the crime —

although in this case no other person was ever
convicted of any part of it.

She was sentenced to fifteen to thirty years. Two
thousand and seven.

Two thousand and eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven. Twelve.
Thirteen. Fourteen.

In those years the appeals ran their course,
the way appeals do, mostly on paper,

mostly slowly. A trial record is reviewed
for errors of law.

It is not a second look at whether the story
was true.

Nothing in the ordinary appellate process
was going to surface a letter

in a prosecutor's file or a scientist's change
of mind. The town went on.

The main street lost another two shopfronts
and gained one.

Children who were at school in two thousand
and six had jobs by two thousand
and fourteen. The ovens stayed cold.
Curtis Haith had been dead for thirteen years,

and the conviction on the books said the matter
was settled.

Nothing about the case changed in any
of those years.
The file was what it had always been.
Three statements that did not agree,
and a bite mark whose timing had moved on request.

The court that reviewed the case recorded
the sentence as fifteen to thirty years.

Whichever number is exact, the shape of it
is the same: at least fifteen years,
and possibly twice that.

That is what a person is handed at the end
of an afternoon in April.

A sentence like that also settles a great many
smaller questions at once.

Where a person will be on every ordinary day
for at least fifteen years.

Which visits are possible and how far someone
has to drive to make them.
What happens to a home, and to the things in it,

and to whoever was depending on her. None
of that appears in a court record.

It is simply the shape the years take once
the number is read out.
On the first of October, two thousand and fifteen,

a judge vacated Crystal Weimer's convictions
and granted her a new trial.

Vacating a conviction does not declare anybody
innocent.

It sets the verdict aside and returns the case
to where it was before the trial.

In principle the Commonwealth can simply try
again.

So on the first of October, two thousand
and fifteen,
Crystal Weimer was not exonerated.
She was back at the start, nine years older,
with the case against her still notionally alive.

What that decision did do was open the file
to people who had not seen it before.

And over the next nine months, one piece
at a time, the case came apart in public.
Joseph Stenger recanted.

He conceded that he had known nothing about Curtis
Haith's murder.

And he said that police had walked him
through his testimony.

The bite-mark expert disavowed what he had told
the jury.
The opinion he had given —

that the mark on Curtis Haith's hand was Crystal
Weimer's —

he now described in two words. "Junk science.
His words, about his own evidence.
That is not this film's assessment.

That is the man who gave the evidence, describing
the evidence he gave.

Then Weimer's lawyers went through the District
Attorney's files,

and they found letters. The letters
were from jailhouse informants.

The same informants who had testified
against her at trial.

At trial, those witnesses had told the jury
that they were not receiving anything

in exchange for their testimony. The letters
showed that they had asked for deals.
And that they may have received them.

There is one question the law expects a jury
to ask about a jailhouse witness.
Are you getting anything for this.
That jury asked it, and they were given an answer,
and the answer was not the whole of it.
Set the withdrawals in order,
because by the middle of two thousand

and sixteen there was very little left holding
the verdict up.

Beal took his account back in two thousand
and four, on the stand,
before the trial existed.

Stenger took his back, and said he had known
nothing at all.

The expert took back the opinion he had given
the jury.

And the men who told that jury they were getting
nothing had written to ask

for something. Every one of those was removed
by the person who had supplied it.
Not by a defence lawyer finding a hole in it.

Not by a new discovery about the night
of the murder.

By the source, in each case, saying it
had not been so.

And an expert was asked to do something nobody
had done since the beginning.
He read Curtis Haith's autopsy report.

Then he looked at the photographs taken of Crystal
Weimer's injuries on the morning

of the twenty-seventh of January, two thousand
and one.

His conclusion was that her injuries
were consistent with her account.

The horseplaying with Gibson, a few days
before the murder.

On the twenty-seventh of June, two thousand
and sixteen,

the charges against Crystal Weimer were dropped
with prejudice.

That is the strongest form the ending of a case
can take.

A case can be dropped and refiled later; a case
dropped with prejudice cannot.

The Commonwealth gave up the right to bring
that charge against her again.
In September of two thousand and seventeen,

Crystal Weimer filed a civil rights lawsuit. She
named Fayette County.

The Office of the Fayette County District
Attorney. The City of Connellsville.

Several Connellsville police officers. One
Pennsylvania State Police officer.
And Nancy Vernon.
That case has taken years of its own,

and most of the years have gone on a question
that is not about what happened
to her at all. It is about who can be sued.
In two thousand and twenty,

a federal appeals court took up what it called
"only a narrow sliver

of this sweeping case".
Not whether the allegations were true.

Whether Vernon could be required to answer them
at all.
The court drew the line where the law draws it.
Approving the criminal complaint was prosecuting,
and for that she was absolutely immune.

But where Weimer alleged that Vernon had acted
as an investigator —

going to the scene, directing officers, assembling
a dive team —
absolute immunity did not cover it.
On two of the claims the court went the other way,

and held that Vernon was entitled to qualified
immunity,

including for directing officers to investigate
the timing of the bite mark.

Qualified immunity is a different instrument
from the absolute kind,

and the two are easy to run together. Absolute
immunity attaches to a function.

If the act was prosecuting, nothing about how it
was done comes into it.

Qualified immunity attaches to the state
of the law.

An official is shielded from a damages claim
unless the conduct broke a rule
that was already clearly established at the time.

So that half of the ruling is narrower than it
sounds.
It is not a finding that the conduct was proper.

It is a finding about what the law had settled
by then.

One more thing about that decision, and it matters
for everything you have heard.

On an appeal at that stage a court does not decide
what is true.

It takes the plaintiff's account as given and asks
whether, if it were all true,

the case could go forward. The court said
so directly.

It accepted the facts as pleaded and drew
the inferences in her favour.

So the account in this film is the account
a federal appeals court was working from,

and the dates and the documents inside it —
the DNA, the recantations, the letters,

the disavowal — are on the record. What
is not settled is what anybody intended.

Go back to the first morning. She told them where
she had been.
Her family said the same.

The blood on her shirt was Gibson's,
and the laboratory confirmed it within weeks.

Nothing at the scene was hers, and what was there
suggested a man.
Fifteen years later,

an expert looked at the photographs
from that morning and said the marks
on her were what she had always said they were.

Everything in between happened anyway.
Not because someone found something.
Nobody ever found anything.

A witness came forward twenty months late
with a detail

that had already been disproved, and then changed
his story twice,

and then took it back on the stand — and the case
went on.

A dentist said she could not tell, and a second
expert was asked instead,

and when the timing did not work the timing
was revised without anyone looking
at anything new.

Crystal Weimer spent more than eleven years
of her life in a prison cell.

Arrested in two thousand and four. Home for six
months.

Convicted in two thousand and six. Cleared in two
thousand and sixteen.

Curtis Haith was killed on the twenty-seventh
of January, two thousand and one.

He was twenty-one years old, and he wanted
to be a chef.

None of what you have heard establishes
who did it.

The convictions being vacated, the charges
being dropped —

that resolves one thing only,
which is that the case against her was not a case.

His killing has never been answered.
That is the second thing this case did.

The first was to take eleven years from a woman
the physical evidence had cleared
in two thousand and one.

The second was that while all of it was going on —
the statements, the retractions,

the revised timing, the trial, the appeal,
the nine years, the letters —

nobody was looking for whoever shot Curtis Haith.
The file had an answer in it.
It had had one since two thousand and four,

when a witness stood up in a courtroom and took it
back.

Everything after that was spent defending
the answer rather than testing it.
